Women's greater access to educational opportunities in medicine, law, business, seminaries, and academia since the 1970s has not resulted in a commensurate movement of women into positions of power in these institutions.
In the early 1990s women made up close to 20 percent of medical faculty, and their chances of receiving tenure were half that of male colleagues.
By the mid-1990s, women accounted for 32 percent of the assistant professors, 21 percent of the associate professors, and 10 percent of the full professors.

The data for this study are a naturalistic set of all the letters of recommendation for successful applicants for faculty positions at a large American medical school over a three-year period from 1992 to 1995.
This amounted to 312 letters for applicants for 103 faculty positions, with sets of approximately three letters per applicant.
By number of words, the average length of the letters was 246 words.
We then analyzed the letters according to the traditional categories of length, naming practices, negative language, and sex-linked terms.
To help visualize length, we standardized all the letters to have lines of 97 characters including spaces.
